Johannes Peter "Honus" Wagner (; February 24, 1874 – December 6, 1955) was an American professional baseball shortstop who played 21 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB) from 1897 to 1917, mostly with the Pittsburgh Pirates.
lead

Nicknamed "the Flying Dutchman" due to his superb speed and German heritage, Wagner was a prototypical five-tool player, known for being a versatile defender who could combine a strong throwing arm with the ability to play almost any defensive position as well as being capable of hitting for average and for power.
lead
He is widely regarded as the greatest shortstop of all time.
lead
In, the Baseball Hall of Fame inducted Wagner as one of the first five members.
lead
At the age of 15, Wagner began his baseball career in the minor leagues in 1889.
lead
After being noticed by a talent scout, he made his MLB debut in 1897 with the Louisville Colonels.
lead
Wagner excelled at playing any position both in the infield and in the outfield, eventually becoming a regular shortstop by 1903.
lead
After the Colonels folded in 1899, club president Barney Dreyfuss bought the Pittsburgh Pirates and brought along Wagner with him, where he would spend the rest of his career.

lead

Robinson broke the color line when he started at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947.
lead
The Dodgers signing Robinson heralded the end of racial segregation in professional baseball, which had relegated black players to the Negro leagues since the 1880s.
lead
Born in Cairo, Georgia, Robinson was raised in Pasadena, California.
lead

A four-sport student athlete at Pasadena Junior College and the University of California, Los Angeles, he was better known for football than he was for baseball, becoming a star with the UCLA Bruins football team.
lead

Following his college career, Robinson was drafted for service during World War II, but was court-martialed for refusing to sit at the back of a segregated Army bus, eventually being honorably discharged.
lead

Shohei Ohtani (, born July 5, 1994) is a Japanese professional baseball designated hitter and pitcher for the Los Angeles Dodgers of Major League Baseball (MLB).
lead
Nicknamed "Shotime", he has previously played in MLB for the Los Angeles Angels and in Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) for the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters.
lead

Because of his contributions as a hitter and as a pitcher, which make him a rare two-way player, Ohtani's prime seasons have been considered among the greatest in baseball history, with some likening them to the early career of Babe Ruth.
lead
Considered early on as an elite two-way player, Ohtani was the first pick of the Fighters in the 2012 NPB draft.
lead
He played for the Fighters from 2013 through 2017 as a pitcher and an outfielder and won the 2016 Japan Series with them.
lead
The Fighters posted Ohtani to MLB after the 2017 season, and he signed with the Angels, soon winning the 2018 American League (AL) Rookie of the Year Award.
lead
Following an injury-plagued 2019 and 2020, Ohtani hit 46 home runs and struck out 156 batters en route to winning his first AL Most Valuable Player Award (MVP) in 2021.
lead
For his statistically unprecedented two-way season, Ohtani received the Commissioner's Historic Achievement Award.
Amateur career

In 2012, Ohtani threw a 160 km/h fastball as an 18-year-old high school pitcher, which at the time, had set a Japanese high school baseball record until it was surpassed by Rōki Sasaki's 163 km/h fastball in 2018.
Amateur career

2013: Rookie season, NPB All-Star
As a pitcher, he finished the season with a 3–0 record in 11 starts.
2013: Rookie season, NPB All-Star
He was the first NPB pitcher since Takao Kajimoto in 1963 to bat 3rd, 4th, or 5th and the first rookie hurler to do so since Junzo Sekine in 1950.
2014: Second NPB All-Star selection
Ohtani pitched 7.0 innings against the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks on August 26, allowing one earned run and striking out nine batters to record his 10th win of the season in a 4–2 victory.
2014: Second NPB All-Star selection

By reaching double digits in both home runs and pitching wins, Ohtani became the first player in NPB history to record at least 10 wins as a pitcher and at least 10 home runs as a batter in the same season.
2014: Second NPB All-Star selection

Ohtani pitched a 1–0 shutout against the Buffaloes on September 13, becoming the first pitcher out of high school to record a 1–0 shutout victory within his first two years for the Fighters since Toshiaki Moriyasu in 1967.
2014: Second NPB All-Star selection

During the July 2014 All-Star Game, Ohtani threw a 162 km/h fastball in the bottom of the first inning, setting a new record for the fastest official pitch thrown by a Japanese pitcher, beating the record set by the Yakult Swallows' Yoshinori Sato in 2010 (161 km/h).
2014: Second NPB All-Star selection
The jersey he wore during the game sold for 1.75 million yen ($), making it the top seller at the All-Star 2014 charity auction.

Of the 15 pitches he threw in the first inning, eight were in the 160s; 99s in MPH.

He was the runaway winner of the 2016 Pacific League Most Valuable Player Award, getting 253 of 254 first-place votes (Naoki Miyanishi got the other one) and one second-place vote.

In 2017, he played in 65 games, hitting.332 with eight homers and 31 RBIs while posting a 3–2 record, a 3.20 ERA, and 29 strikeouts as a pitcher.
2017: Final season in the NPB
The injury had originally occurred in the 2016 Japan Series and had cost him a chance to play in the 2017 World Baseball Classic in addition to restricting his playing time during the season.

This capped his bonus at $3.557 million and limited him to a rookie salary scale, while the signing team also had to pay a $20 million posting fee to the Fighters.

On June 8, he was placed on the injured list for the first time in his MLB career due to a Grade 2 UCL sprain in his right elbow.

2020: Continued injury struggles

2020: Continued injury struggles

2021: Unanimous AL MVP

In the last game of the season against the Seattle Mariners, he passed teammate Mike Trout's 45 home runs in a single season to finish with the second-most home runs in a season in Angels history at 46, trailing only Troy Glaus' 47 home runs in 2000.
2021: Unanimous AL MVP

2021: Unanimous AL MVP

For the 2021 All-MLB Team, Ohtani became the first player to be named to both First and Second teams, in the same season (as a designated hitter and starting pitcher, respectively).

2022: AL MVP finalist, two-way dominance

2022: AL MVP finalist, two-way dominance

Ohtani also led the majors with a home-to-first average time of 4.09 seconds and was the only player in the majors to tally at least six triples and 34 home runs in 2022 (making him the first player to do so in a second consecutive year).

In connection with his $7.85 million home purchase, Ohtani established an LLC named "Decopin", which he named after his dog.
Endorsements and mass media coverage
In 2021, Ohtani was named to Time 100's list of most influential people of 2021 and awarded the Commissioner's Historic Achievement Award by Commissioner Rob Manfred.
Endorsements and mass media coverage

In 2023, Ohtani endorsement earnings were estimated to be an MLB league-leading $35–40 million, up from his MLB league-leading $20 million endorsement earnings in 2022, which tripled from his MLB league-leading $6 million endorsement earnings in 2021.

By 2025, his estimated endorsements had risen to $100 million for the year.
Endorsements and mass media coverage

Interpreter gambling scandal
In February 2025, Mizuhara was sentenced to repay Ohtani $17 million along with a 57-month prison sentence.

(May 6, 1931 – June 18, 2024), nicknamed "the Say Hey Kid", was an American professional baseball center fielder who played 23 major league seasons.
lead

Widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, Mays was a five-tool player who began his career in the Negro leagues, playing for the Birmingham Black Barons, and spent the rest of his career in the National League (NL), playing for the New York / San Francisco Giants and New York Mets.
lead
Born in Westfield, Alabama, Mays was an all-around athlete.
lead
He joined the Black Barons of the Negro American League in 1948, playing with them until the Giants signed him upon his graduation from high school in 1950.
lead
He debuted in the National League with the Giants and won the Rookie of the Year Award in 1951 after hitting 20 home runs to help the Giants win their first pennant in 14 years.
lead
In 1954, he won the NL Most Valuable Player (MVP) Award, leading the Giants to their last World Series title before their move to the West Coast.
lead
His over-the-shoulder catch in Game 1 of the 1954 World Series is one of the most famous baseball plays of all time.
lead
After the Giants moved to San Francisco, Mays went on to win another MVP Award in 1965 and also led the Giants to the 1962 World Series, this time losing to the New York Yankees.
Early life
Though he turned 18 in 1949, Mays did not graduate from Fairfield until 1950, which journalist Allen Barra calls "a minor mystery in Willie's life".

Sanford Koufax (; né Braun; born December 30, 1935), nicknamed "the Left Arm of God", is an American former professional baseball player.

lead

lead
Retiring at age 30 due to chronic pain in his pitching elbow, Koufax was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1972 at age 36, the youngest player ever elected.
lead
Born in Brooklyn, New York, Koufax was primarily a basketball player in his youth and had pitched in only a few games before signing with the Brooklyn Dodgers at age 19.
lead
Due to the bonus rule he signed under, Koufax never pitched in the minor leagues.
lead
His lack of pitching experience caused manager Walter Alston to distrust Koufax, who saw inconsistent playing time during his first six seasons.

On May 10, 2007, Griffey hit his sixth home run of the season and the 569th of his career, tying Rafael Palmeiro for ninth place on the career home runs list.
Griffey tied Harmon Killebrew for eighth on the all-time list hitting his 573rd career home run on May 22.
On June 22, 2007, Griffey made his first return to Seattle after his trade to the Reds.

Many of the fans in attendance made signs professing their gratitude and adoration toward him with quotes such as: "The House that Griffey Built", "Seattle Junior", and "Griffey we miss you." Griffey went 1-for-5 in the game.
On June 24, Griffey hit his 583rd and 584th career home runs, tying and passing Mark McGwire for seventh place on the all-time career home run list.
Following the Cincinnati Reds versus Seattle Mariners series from June 22–24, 2007, a fan movement emerged petitioning Mariners' management to bring Griffey back.
Griffey received the most votes of any player in the National League for the 2007 All-Star balloting, and in the July 10 game, he went on to drive in two runs for the National League.
On July 16, 2007, Griffey hit his 587th home run to pass Frank Robinson for sixth place on the all-time home run list.
On July 18, 2007, Griffey hit his 2,500th hit, a first-inning single off Atlanta Braves starting pitcher John Smoltz.
On September 19, 2007, in a game against the Chicago Cubs, Griffey fielded a Derrek Lee single in right field, then suddenly went down in pain.
On August 22, 2007, Griffey was selected as an all-time Rawlings Gold Glove winner, on a list of nine players considered the greatest defensive players in the last 50 years.
On April 4, 2008, Griffey passed Reggie Jackson for 16th on the all-time list after driving in his 1,702nd run.
On June 9, Griffey hit his 600th home run on a 3–1 pitch from Mark Hendrickson of the Florida Marlins in the first inning at Land Shark Stadium in Miami.

Despite being ranked second in the National League All-Star voting for outfielders for most of the first half of the season, Griffey finished fourth with 2,907,746 ballots, 87,000 votes behind Kosuke Fukudome.
At the All-Star Break, Griffey was batting.239 with 12 home runs and 42 RBI.
On July 30, Griffey hit his 608th career home run in his last game for the Reds.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
On July 31, 2008, at the MLB trade deadline, Griffey was traded to the Chicago White Sox for pitcher Nick Masset and infielder Danny Richar, ending his nine-year tenure in Cincinnati.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
In his first game with the White Sox, he went 2-for-3 with 2 RBI, a walk, and a run.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
On August 20, 2008, Griffey hit his first home run as a member of the White Sox, off the Mariners' R.
Chicago White Sox (2008)

Griffey's signature moment with the White Sox came on September 30, the last game of the 2008 season; an extra 163rd game between the White Sox and Minnesota Twins to break the tie atop the AL Central.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
The White Sox went on to beat the Twins, 1–0, to advance to the 2008 American League Division Series, where they fell to the Tampa Bay Rays.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
On October 30, 2008, the White Sox declined a $16 million option on Griffey, making him a free agent for the first time in his career.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
Griffey received a buyout for $4 million, split between the Reds and White Sox.
Chicago White Sox (2008)
Griffey hit.249 with 18 home runs and 71 RBI during 143 games with the Reds and White Sox in 2008.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
Griffey went 1-for-3 with a home run in his regular-season debut on April against the Minnesota Twins.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
The home run was Griffey's eighth Opening Day home run; as of 2025, he is tied with Frank Robinson and Adam Dunn for first place in this category.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)

On April 15, 2009, Griffey hit his 400th home run as a Mariner (613th of career), off Los Angeles Angels pitcher Jered Weaver, becoming the first MLB player to hit 400 home runs with one club (Mariners) and 200 home runs with another (Reds).
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
On June 23, 2009, at Safeco Field, Griffey hit the 5,000th home run in franchise history, off San Diego Padres pitcher Chad Gaudin.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
On July 1, Griffey hit career home run 621 at the new Yankee Stadium, off Yankees pitcher Andy Pettitte in the sixth inning.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
On August 12, 2009, against his former team, the Chicago White Sox, he hit a run-scoring single in the bottom of the 14th inning to win the game, 1–0, for the Mariners.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
Griffey returned to the Mariners for the 2010 campaign with a similar one-year contract to that of 2009, but struggled offensively over the first two months while posting a.184 batting average.
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)
On May 20, in a game against the Toronto Blue Jays, Griffey hit a run-scoring single off Blue Jays' closer Kevin Gregg to win the game, 4–3, for the Mariners.
Post-playing career
Griffey joined Alvin Davis (1997), Dave Niehaus (2000), Jay Buhner (2004), Edgar Martínez (2007), Randy Johnson (2012) and Dan Wilson (2012).
Post-playing career
Writer Bill Simmons pointed out the prevalent belief that Griffey was the best home run hitter of the 1990s who everyone was convinced never used performance enhancing drugs.
Post-playing career
In 2018, The Seattle Times named Griffey as the most important athlete in Seattle sports history.
Post-playing career
On October 25, 2021, Griffey joined the Mariners ownership group, becoming the first former player to hold partnership interest in the Mariners.
Baseball Hall of Fame election
On January 6, 2016, Griffey was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame, receiving 99.32 percent of the vote, breaking the record previously held by Tom Seaver's 98.84 percent in 1992.
Baseball Hall of Fame election
(Mariano Rivera later became the first unanimous inductee in 2019.) A flag bearing Griffey's number 24 was flown from Seattle's Space Needle following the announcement.
Baseball Hall of Fame election
The other three are Chipper Jones, who was inducted in 2018, Harold Baines, who was inducted by the Veterans Committee in 2019, and Joe Mauer, who was inducted in 2024.
Baseball Hall of Fame election
Coinciding with his Hall of Fame election, the Mariners announced on January 8, 2016, that they would retire his jersey number 24.
Baseball Hall of Fame election

The Mariners also honored Griffey in a unique fashion in the 2016 MLB draft, selecting his son Trey in the 24th round (matching his jersey number), even though Trey, at the time a wide receiver at the University of Arizona, had not played baseball since his preteen years.
Personal life
On May 26, 2024, Griffey drove the pace car for the Indianapolis 500.

(born January 31, 1947), nicknamed "the Ryan Express", is an American former professional baseball pitcher and sports executive.
lead
Over a record 27-year playing career in Major League Baseball (MLB), Ryan pitched for the New York Mets, California Angels, Houston Astros, and Texas Rangers.
lead
After his retirement in 1993, Ryan was chief executive officer (CEO) of the Texas Rangers and an executive advisor to the Houston Astros.
lead
He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1999 in his first year of eligibility, and is widely considered to be one of the greatest pitchers of all time.
lead
Ryan was a right-handed power pitcher who consistently threw pitches that were clocked above 100 miles per hour (161 km/h), being one of the first pitchers to officially be able to do so.
lead
He maintained this velocity throughout his pitching career, being known as one of the top pitchers in Major League Baseball into his mid-40s.
lead
Ryan was also known to throw a devastating 12–6 curveball at exceptional velocity for a breaking ball.
lead
Ryan had a lifetime win–loss record of 324–292 (.526) and was an eight-time All-Star.
Early life
Lynn Nolan Ryan Jr. was born on January 31, 1947, in Refugio, Texas, a small town located just south of Victoria in the southern part of the state.
Early life
Ryan was the youngest of six children born to Martha Lee (née Hancock; 1913–1990) and Lynn Nolan Ryan Sr.
Early life
The senior Ryan operated a newspaper delivery service for the Houston Post that required him to rise in the early morning hours to prepare 1,500 newspapers for delivery over a 55 mi route.
Early life
Ryan joined Alvin Little League Baseball when he was nine, made the all-star team when he was 11 and 12, and pitched the first no-hitter of his life a few years later.
Early life
Ryan held the school's single game strikeout record for 44 years, striking out 21 hitters in a seven-inning game.
Early life
The record was tied by Alvin High School pitchers Aaron Stewart and Josh Land in the same week in 2009.
Early life
In 1963, at an Alvin High School game at Clear Creek High School in League City, Texas, Red Murff, a scout for the New York Mets, first noticed sophomore pitcher Ryan.
Early life

In his subsequent report to the Mets, Murff stated that Ryan had "the best arm I've seen in my life." As a senior in 1965, Ryan had a 19–3 record and led the Alvin Yellow Jackets to the Texas high school state finals.
Draft and minor leagues
After he graduated from Alvin, the New York Mets selected Ryan in the 12th round, with the 295th overall pick, of the 1965 Major League Baseball draft.
Draft and minor leagues
Overall, he was 6–9 in 1965 with a 4.33 earned run average (ERA) and 150 strikeouts in 120 innings.
Draft and minor leagues
In 1966, Ryan pitched for the Class A Greenville Mets of the Western Carolinas League, where he went 17–2 with a 2.51 ERA and 272 strikeouts in 183 innings.
Draft and minor leagues
Overall, Ryan had 307 strikeouts in 202 minor league innings in 1966, earning a late-season call-up to the New York Mets.
Draft and minor leagues
In 34 total innings, Ryan had 54 strikeouts in 1967.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
When Ryan was called up by the New York Mets in 1966, he was the second-youngest player in the league.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
Playing in two games, his first strikeout was Pat Jarvis, and he gave up his first major league home run to Joe Torre.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
Ryan missed much of the 1967 season due to illness, an arm injury, and service with the Army Reserve; he pitched only seven innings for the Mets' minor league affiliate in Jacksonville.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
In the 1968 season, Ryan returned to the major leagues, where he stayed until his retirement in 1993.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)

Against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Championship Series (NLCS), Ryan completed a Mets sweep by throwing seven innings of relief in Game 3, getting his first playoff win (it took him 12 years to get another).
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
Then in the 1969 World Series, Ryan saved Game 3, pitching shutout innings against the Baltimore Orioles.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
The Game 3 victory gave the Mets a 2–1 lead in the Series, which they went on to win in five games.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
On April 18, 1970, Ryan tied a Mets record by striking out 15 batters in one game.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
Four days later, Ryan's teammate Seaver topped it with a then-MLB record 19 against the San Diego Padres (Ryan tied this record four years later).
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
His ERA for the first half of the 1971 season was 2.24; in the second half, it was 7.74., this was the steepest second half increase in ERA for a starting pitcher in MLB history.
New York Mets (1966, 1968–1971)
In five seasons with the Mets, 105 games and 74 starts, Ryan had a 29–38 record, with a 3.58 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, with 344 walks and 493 strikeouts in 511 innings.
California Angels (1972–1979)

On December 10, 1971, the 24-year-old Ryan was traded to the California Angels along with pitcher Don Rose, catcher Francisco Estrada, and outfielder Leroy Stanton for shortstop Jim Fregosi (who later managed Ryan in Anaheim).
California Angels (1972–1979)

In his first season with the Angels, Ryan was given a chance to pitch regularly as a starter for the first time in his career, mainly because by then he had fulfilled his military obligation and no longer had to commute to Houston every other week.
California Angels (1972–1979)
He had a league-leading 329 strikeouts—nearly a third more than the AL runner-up, and the fourth-highest total of the 20th century to that point.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Within five seasons, the season was only Ryan's fourth-highest strikeout total.
California Angels (1972–1979)

He also set a still-standing Major League record by allowing 5.26 hits per nine innings, breaking Luis Tiant's 5.30 in 1968, as well as posting a 2.28 earned run average that year, to date the second-lowest in franchise history, trailing only Dean Chance's 1.65 in 1964.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Though Ryan's actual winning percentage hovered only slightly over.500, his strikeouts and no-hitters brought him media attention.
California Angels (1972–1979)

Although the Angels were a sub-.500 team and remained one for much of Ryan's time with them, he managed to post some winning records, notably 19–16 in 1972, 21–16 in 1973, and 22–16 in 1974 (the 22 wins tied what remains the Angels franchise record, set by Clyde Wright in 1970).
California Angels (1972–1979)
Ryan also led the league in losses in 1976 with a 17–18 record (one short of the franchise record for losses).
California Angels (1972–1979)
In the early 1970s, many teams used a four-man rotation and expected the starter to complete the game; thus most of the games Ryan started ended in a decision.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Ryan threw a no-hitter against the Kansas City Royals on May 15, 1973.
California Angels (1972–1979)
He threw a second no-hitter on July 15 against the Detroit Tigers, he struck out 17 batters – the most in a recorded no-hitter.
California Angels (1972–1979)
(This record was later tied by Max Scherzer on October 3, 2015.) Ryan was so dominant in this game, it led to one of baseball's best-remembered pranks.
California Angels (1972–1979)
In 1973, Ryan set his first major record when he struck out 383 batters in one season, beating Sandy Koufax's old mark by one.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Pitching 13 innings against the Boston Red Sox on June 14, 1974, Ryan threw 235 pitches, striking out 19, walking 10 and getting a no-decision.
California Angels (1972–1979)
During a September 7, 1974, game against the Chicago White Sox at Anaheim Stadium, Ryan became the first Major League pitcher to have his pitch speed measured during a game.
California Angels (1972–1979)
A primitive radar gun clocked a ninth-inning fastball at 100.8 mph when it was 10 ft in front of home plate.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Ryan added a third no-hitter in 1974 and a fourth in 1975, tying another of Koufax's records.
California Angels (1972–1979)
In 1974 he twice struck out 19 batters, tying Tom Seaver and Steve Carlton for the single-game record for a nine-inning game.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Roger Clemens became the first pitcher with a 20-strikeout game in 1986.
California Angels (1972–1979)

Ryan led the American League in strikeouts seven times during his eight seasons with the Angels, but he also led the league in walks in six of those years, and finished second the other two seasons: 1975 and 1979.
California Angels (1972–1979)
Aside from Bob Feller in 1938, Ryan is the only man since 1900 to walk 200 batters in a season, which he did twice: in 1974 and 1977.
California Angels (1972–1979)

Though Ryan's strikeouts and no-hitters got him considerable media attention, he did not persuade Angels general manager Buzzie Bavasi, who dismissed him as a flashy.500 pitcher (Ryan was 26–27 in the last two years he was with the Angels).
California Angels (1972–1979)
In his eight seasons with the Angels, Ryan was 138–121, a 3.07 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, with 1,302 walks and 2,416 strikeouts in 2181 innings over 288 starts and 156 complete games.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
On November 19, 1979, Ryan signed a four-year contract worth $4.5 million (equivalent to $ million in ) with the Houston Astros, becoming MLB's first million-dollar player.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
In a nationally televised game against the Los Angeles Dodgers on April 12, 1980, Ryan hit a three-run home run off Don Sutton.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
On July 4 at Riverfront Stadium, Ryan recorded his 3,000th career strikeout, the victim being César Gerónimo of the Cincinnati Reds.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
In the fifth and final game of the series, Ryan and the Astros held a 5–2 lead entering the 8th inning.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
The Houston bullpen allowed the Phillies to take a 7–5 lead, and only a game-tying Astro rally permitted Ryan to escape the loss.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
On September 26, 1981, Ryan threw his fifth no-hitter, breaking Koufax's mark while becoming the third pitcher to throw a no-hitter in each league.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
By the end of the 1982 season, both Ryan and Steve Carlton were approaching Walter Johnson's all-time strikeout record, sometimes passing one another's career totals in successive starts.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
On April 27, 1983, Ryan won the race with his 3,509th whiff, against Brad Mills of the Montreal Expos.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
(Carlton reached the same mark two weeks after Ryan, and Gaylord Perry did so later that season.) On July 11, 1985, Ryan struck out Danny Heep for his 4,000th career strikeout.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
Despite his.333 winning percentage, Ryan tied for 5th place in the 1987 Cy Young voting.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)
Ryan hit his second and final career home run in a 12–3 win on May 1, 1987, against the Atlanta Braves.
Houston Astros (1980–1988)

In nine seasons as a pitcher with the Astros (his longest tenure with any team), Ryan compiled a 106–94 record in 282 starts, a 3.13 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, with 796 walks and 1,866 strikeouts in 1,854 innings.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Oliver's father Bob had also been a teammate of Ryan's, with the Angels from 1972 to 1974.) In 1989, he went 16–10 and led the league with 301 strikeouts.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Against the Oakland Athletics on August 22, Ryan struck out Rickey Henderson, becoming the only pitcher to record 5,000 career strikeouts.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Two years later, at 44, Ryan finished fifth in the league in ERA (2.91) and third in strikeouts (203).
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
In 1990, Ryan threw his sixth no-hitter on June 11 against the Athletics, and earned his 300th win on July 31 against the Milwaukee Brewers, and was named The Sporting News Sportsman of the Year.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
On May 1, 1991, at age 44, Ryan extended his record by throwing the seventh no-hitter of his career, striking out Roberto Alomar of the Toronto Blue Jays for the final out.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
On August 6, 1992, Ryan had the only ejection of his career after engaging in a shouting match with Oakland Athletics outfielder Willie Wilson with two outs in the eighth inning.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Ryan's last start was his career-worst; he allowed a single, four walks, and a grand slam in the bottom of the first without recording an out.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Ryan left trailing 5–0, and was eventually charged with the loss in a 7–4 defeat; Ryan's fourth walk was completed after his injury by reliever Steve Dreyer, but charged to Ryan.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Greg Myers of the California Angels was the last strikeout victim of Nolan Ryan's career, on September 17, 1993.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
Ryan finished his career having played in the major leagues a record of 27 seasons.
Texas Rangers (1989–1993)
In five seasons with the Rangers, Ryan had a 51–39 record, a 3.43 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, with 353 walks and 939 strikeouts in 840 innings over 129 starts.
Seven no-hitters
In those seven games, Ryan accumulated a total of 94 strikeouts and 26 walks; a ratio of 3.6 strikeouts per walk (his career K:BB was 2.0).
Seven no-hitters
Ryan struck out 17 in his no-hitter on July 15, 1973, versus Detroit and walked eight in his subsequent no-hitter against Minnesota, both respective highs for his no-hitters.
Later activity

When the Texas Rangers moved to The Ballpark in Arlington during the 1994 season, he threw the ceremonial first pitch for an exhibition game between the Rangers and the New York Mets for the stadium's soft opening day on April 1, 1994.
Later activity
Ryan threw out the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3 of the 2005 World Series between the Astros and the White Sox, the first World Series game played in Texas.
Later activity
That game went 14 innings, equaling the longest in innings in World Series history (at 5 hours and 41 minutes, it was the longest in time).
Texas Rangers president and CEO (2008–2013)

At midnight on August 5, 2010, the Ryan/Greenberg group, Rangers Baseball Express, was announced as the winner of the final auction to purchase the Rangers, after final approval from Major League Baseball.
Texas Rangers president and CEO (2008–2013)
The final cash bid to purchase the franchise was $385 million.
Texas Rangers president and CEO (2008–2013)
Ryan was named the Dallas–Fort Worth's 2012 CEO of the Year by Southern Methodist University's Cox School of Business.
Texas Rangers president and CEO (2008–2013)
On October 17, 2013, Ryan announced that he was stepping down as Rangers CEO effective October 31, 2013.
Legacy
(He is tied with Cap Anson for the most all time.) Ryan ranks first for all-time in strikeouts (5,714), fewest hits allowed per nine innings (6.56), and no-hitters (7).
Legacy
Ryan had 15 or more strikeouts in a game 26 times, second to Randy Johnson, who had 28.
Legacy
Bush, and Bill Clinton—equaling a 20th-century record that had been set by Jim Kaat.
Legacy

Ryan also ranks high on the list for four "negative" records; he ranks first all-time in walks allowed (2,795), first in wild pitches (277), third in losses (292 – most in the post-1920 live-ball era), and ninth in batters hit (158).
Legacy
Ryan was the first pitcher in MLB history to give up ten grand slam home runs, including one to Dann Howitt, the next-to-last batter Ryan faced in his career; that record has since been surpassed.
Legacy

In another column, Neyer, while stating that Ryan belonged in the Hall of Fame, pointed to Ryan's record-breaking walks total and noted that his.309 on-base percentage against "wasn't even close to being in the top 100".
Legacy
The California Angels retired the number 30 on June 16, 1992; the Texas Rangers retired his number 34 on September 15, 1996; and the Houston Astros retired number 34 on September 29, 1996.
Legacy
(99.32%, 437 out of 440 possible), and Tom Seaver (98.84%, 425 out of 430 possible).
Legacy
In 1999, he ranked 41st on The Sporting News list of the 100 Greatest Baseball Players and was elected to the Major League Baseball All-Century Team.
Legacy
In 2020, The Athletic ranked Ryan at number 50 on its "Baseball 100" list, complied by sportswriter Joe Posnanski.
Legacy

In 1992, the United States Mint produced a $1 commemorative coin honoring Olympic baseball depicting a pitcher in a USA Baseball uniform in a pose nearly identical to Ryan's photo on his 1991 Fleer baseball card.

Derek Sanderson Jeter (; born June 26, 1974), nicknamed "the Captain", is an American former professional baseball player, businessman, and baseball executive.
lead
A shortstop, Jeter spent his entire 20-year Major League Baseball (MLB) career with the New York Yankees.
lead

He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility in 2020; he received 396 of 397 possible votes, the second-highest percentage in MLB history (behind only teammate Mariano Rivera) and the highest by a position player (both records since tied by Ichiro Suzuki).
lead
He was the chief executive officer (CEO) and part owner of the league's Miami Marlins from September 2017 to February 2022.
lead

A five-time World Series champion with the Yankees, Jeter is regarded as a central contributor to the franchise's dynasty during the late 1990s and early 2000s for his hitting, base-running, fielding, and leadership.
lead
He is the Yankees' all-time career leader in hits (3,465), doubles (544), games played (2,747), stolen bases (358), times on base (4,716), plate appearances (12,602) and at bats (11,195).
lead
His accolades include 14 All-Star selections, five Gold Glove Awards, five Silver Slugger Awards, two Hank Aaron Awards, and a 2009 Roberto Clemente Award.
lead

Jeter was the 28th player to reach 3,000 hits and finished his career sixth in MLB history in career hits (3,465), second all-time among right-handed hitters behind Hank Aaron, and first among shortstops.
Early life and education

In his senior year, he batted.508 and compiled 23 runs batted in (RBIs), 21 walks, four home runs, a.637 on-base percentage (OBP), a.831 slugging percentage (SLG), 12 stolen bases (in 12 attempts), and only one strikeout.
Draft
Fearing Jeter would insist on a salary bonus of at least $1 million to forgo college for a professional contract, they chose Cal State Fullerton outfielder Phil Nevin, who signed for $700,000.
Minor leagues
In his first professional game, he failed to get a hit in seven at-bats, going 0-for-7, while striking out five times.
Minor leagues
He batted.247 in his first 11 games with Greensboro, and struggled defensively, making nine errors in 48 chances.
Minor leagues
Baseball America rated him among the top 100 prospects in baseball before the 1993 season, ranking him 44th.
Minor leagues

Returning to the Hornets in 1993, his first full season of professional baseball, Jeter hit.295 with five home runs, 71 RBIs, and 18 stolen bases; SAL managers voted him the "Most Outstanding Major League Prospect" in the league.
Minor leagues
He finished second in the SAL in triples (11), third in hits (152), and 11th in batting average, and was named to the postseason All-Star team. he committed 56 errors, a SAL record.
Minor leagues

During the 1994–95 Major League Baseball strike, Gene Michael, the Yankees' general manager, offered Jeter the opportunity to work out for the MLB team with replacement players in spring training before the 1995 season.
He was assigned uniform number 2, which was most recently worn by Mike Gallego from 1992 to 1994.
The following day, he recorded his first two major league hits and scored his first two career runs.

After Fernández batted a disappointing.245 and appeared in only 108 games due to injuries in 1995, newly hired Yankees manager Joe Torre turned to Jeter for the 1996 season, hoping for a.250 batting average and dependable defense.

Rated the sixth-best prospect in baseball by Baseball America heading into the 1996 season, Jeter started on Opening Day, the first Yankee rookie to start as shortstop for the team since Tom Tresh in 1962.
By year's end, Jeter batted.314 with 10 home runs, 104 runs scored, and 78 RBIs.
He was named the unanimous AL Rookie of the Year, receiving all 28 first-place votes in only the fifth sweep in the honor's 50-year history.
The Yankees defeated the Atlanta Braves in the 1996 World Series to win their first championship since the 1978 World Series.
Rodriguez, the first overall selection in the 1993 MLB draft, first contacted Jeter about his experiences as a high first-round pick.
Before the 1997 season, Jeter and the Yankees agreed on a $540,000 contract with performance bonuses.
Becoming the Yankees' leadoff batter, Jeter batted.291, with 10 home runs, 70 RBIs, 116 runs, and 190 hits.

In the regular season, he batted.324 with a league-leading 127 runs, 19 home runs, and 84 RBIs, for a team that won 114 games during the regular season and is widely considered to be one of the greatest of all time.
In the playoffs, Jeter hit only.176 in the 1998 ALDS and ALCS, but batted.353 in the World Series, as the Yankees defeated the San Diego Padres in four games.
Eligible for salary arbitration for the first time before the 1999 season, Jeter was awarded a $5 million salary.
In the postseason, Jeter batted.455 in the ALDS,.350 in the ALCS, and.353 in the World Series, as the Yankees defeated the Braves to win another championship.
During the 1999–2000 offseason, the Yankees negotiated with Jeter, tentatively agreeing to a seven-year, $118.5 million contract.

However, because Steinbrenner did not want to set a record for the largest contract, the Yankees waited while Juan González and the Detroit Tigers negotiated on a reported eight-year, $143 million contract extension.
To avoid arbitration, Jeter and the Yankees agreed to a one-year deal worth $10 million.
Jeter batted a team-best.339 in the 2000 regular season and added 15 home runs, 73 RBIs, 119 runs scored, and 22 stolen bases.

During the postseason, he batted only.211 in the ALDS against the Oakland Athletics, but rebounded to hit.318 in the Championship Series against the Seattle Mariners, and.409 in the World Series against the New York Mets.
Jeter won the World Series MVP Award, becoming the first (and so far only) player to win the All-Star Game MVP and World Series MVP Awards in the same season.
With one year remaining until he would become eligible for free agency, Jeter signed a ten-year, $189 million contract before the 2001 season to remain with the Yankees.
Alex Rodriguez had signed a ten-year, $252 million contract with the Texas Rangers earlier in the offseason, setting the market for Jeter's negotiations.
Jeter became the second-highest-paid athlete across all team sports and auto racing, trailing only Rodriguez.
The $18.9 million average annual value of Jeter's contract was the third-highest in baseball, behind only Rodriguez ($25.2 million) and Manny Ramirez ($20 million).
In 2001, Jeter batted.311 with 21 home runs, 74 RBIs, 110 runs scored, and 27 stolen bases.
The play, known as "The Flip", was later voted seventh in Baseball Weeklys 10 Most Amazing Plays of all time, and won the 2002 Best Play ESPY Award.
Jeter batted.297, with 18 home runs, 75 RBIs, 124 runs scored, 191 hits, and a career-best 32 stolen bases during the 2002 regular season.

lead

lead

lead
A switch hitter, Rose remains the MLB's all-time leader in hits (4,256), games played (3,562), at-bats (14,053), singles (3,215), and outs (10,328).
lead
He won three World Series championships, three batting titles, two Gold Glove Awards, a Most Valuable Player Award, and a Rookie of the Year Award.
lead
He made 17 All-Star appearances in an unequaled five positions (second baseman, left fielder, right fielder, third baseman, and first baseman).
lead

Early years
The Colt.45s lost the game in the bottom of the ninth inning, and Ken Johnson became the first major league pitcher to lose a complete game no-hitter.

lead

lead
In the 2010s, Topps was the only baseball card manufacturer with a license with Major League Baseball.
lead
After Topps lost the license to Fanatics, Inc. in 2022, Fanatics acquired Topps.

Topps was founded in 1938 by four brothers, Abram, Ira, Philip and Joseph Shorin.
Beginnings and consolidation
Topps' most successful early product was Bazooka bubble gum, which was packaged with a small comic on the wrapper.

The Shorins, in recognition of his negotiation abilities, sent Sy to London in 1964 to negotiate the rights for Topps to produce Beatles trading cards.

Incorporation

Many of the oil paintings for the sets were rendered by artist Gerry Dvorak, who also worked as an animator for Famous Studios.

Until 2019, Topps made Topps Premier League stickers and the Match Attax trading card game, and since 2015 it has produced stickers and trading cards for the UEFA Champions League.

sents: lead
Fleer/Skybox International LP was an American manufacturing company.
lead
Established as Fleer Corporation by Frank H.
lead
Fleer in 1885, it was the first company to successfully manufacture bubble gum, remaining a family-owned enterprise until 1989.
lead
Fleer originally developed a bubble gum formulation called Blibber-Blubber in 1906.
lead
While this gum could be blown into bubbles, in other respects it was vastly inferior to regular chewing gum, and Blibber-Blubber was never marketed to the public.
lead
In 1928, Fleer employee Walter Diemer improved the Blibber-Blubber formulation to produce the first commercially successful bubble gum, Dubble Bubble.
lead
Its pink color set a tradition for nearly all bubble gums to follow.
lead
Fleer became known as a maker of sports cards, starting in 1923 with the production of baseball cards.
Beginning and early card attempts

Well established as a gum and candy company, Fleer predated many of its competitors into the business of issuing sports cards with its 1923 release of baseball cards in its "Bobs and Fruit Hearts" candy product.
Beginning and early card attempts
These rare cards are basically the same as the 1923 W515 strip cards but are machine cut and have a printed ad for the candy company on the back.
Beginning and early card attempts
Many years later in 1959 it signed baseball star Ted Williams to a contract and sold an 80-card set oriented around highlights of his career.
Beginning and early card attempts
Fleer was unable to include other players because rival company Topps had signed most active baseball players to exclusive contracts.
Beginning and early card attempts
Williams was nearing the end of his career and retired after the 1960 season.
Beginning and early card attempts
One set was produced in 1960 and a second in 1961.
Beginning and early card attempts
The company did not produce new cards the next year, but continued selling the 1961 set while it focused on signing enough players to produce a set featuring active players in 1963.
Beginning and early card attempts

This 67-card set included a number of stars, including 1962 National League MVP Maury Wills (then holder of the modern record for stolen bases in a season), who had elected to sign with Fleer instead of Topps.
Beginning and early card attempts
Topps still held the rights to most players and the set was not particularly successful.
Beginning and early card attempts
In 1961, each company produced cards featuring players from both leagues.
Beginning and early card attempts
In 1964, Philadelphia Gum secured the rights for NFL cards and Topps took over the AFL.
Beginning and early card attempts
Sometime after 1961 Fleer produced The Three Stooges' cards.
Legal battles
A hearing examiner ruled against Topps in 1965, but the Commission reversed this decision on appeal.
Legal battles
The Commission concluded that because the contracts only covered the sale of cards with gum, competition was still possible by selling cards with other small, low-cost products.
Legal battles
Fleer chose not to pursue such options and instead sold its remaining player contracts to Topps for $395,000 in 1966 ($3,344,211.42 in 2021 dollars).
Legal battles
In 1968, Fleer was approached by the Major League Baseball Players Association, a recently organized players' union, about obtaining a group license to produce cards.
Legal battles
The MLBPA was in a dispute with Topps over player contracts, and offered Fleer the exclusive rights to market cards of most players starting in 1973, when many of Topps's contracts would expire.
Legal battles
Fleer returned to the union in September 1974 with a proposal to sell 5-by-7-inch satin patches of players, somewhat larger than normal baseball cards.
Legal battles
By now, the MLBPA had settled its differences with Topps and reached an agreement that gave Topps a right of first refusal on such offers.
Legal battles
In April 1975, Fleer asked for Topps to waive its exclusive rights and allow Fleer to produce stickers, stamps, or other small items featuring active baseball players.
Legal battles
Topps refused, and Fleer then sued both Topps and the MLBPA to break the Topps monopoly.
Legal battles

After several years of litigation, the Topps monopoly on baseball cards was finally broken by a lawsuit decided by federal judge Clarence Charles Newcomer in 1980, in which the judge ended Topps's exclusive right to sell baseball cards with gum, allowing Fleer to compete in the market.
Legal battles
Fleer and another company, Donruss, were thus allowed to begin making cards in 1981.
Key card sets
In 1984, Fleer was the only major trading card manufacturer to release a Roger Clemens card; they included the then-Boston Red Sox prospect in their 1984 Fleer Baseball Update Set.
Key card sets
The 1984 update set also included the first licensed card of Hall Of Fame outfielder Kirby Puckett.
Key card sets
Fleer also released factory sets of their baseball cards from 1986–92.
Key card sets
The 1986 set was not sealed, but the 1987–89 sets were sealed with a sticker and the 1990–92 sets were shrink-wrapped.
Key card sets
From 1987–89, Fleer also released a parallel baseball set on glossy paper.
Key card sets
The set also included an additional 11 card All Star sticker set featuring a second rookie card and sticker of Michael Jordan.
Key card sets
From 1986-1988, Fleer was the only major card company that produced basketball cards.
Key card sets
In 1989, Hoops released a two-part release, while Fleer continued with their singular release approach.
Key card sets
In 1990, SkyBox, Topps, and Upper Deck introduced their own basketball card sets in two major releases each year per company.
Acquisitions and later days
The Fleer family, Frank Fleer's descendants, sold Fleer in 1989 for just under US$70,000,000 to John W.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer was pushing into retail chains like Rite Aid, which brought the ire of the hobby dealers in the early 1990s.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer's first Ultra set came out in 1991.
Acquisitions and later days
The 1991 set had an announced production of 15% of regular Fleer and was produced on higher quality card stock using silver ink.
Acquisitions and later days
The 1992 set used UV coating on both sides and gold foil stamping on the front.
Acquisitions and later days

1994's Ultra and regular Fleer sets began another tradition of offering an insert card in every pack; in 1995 they started another tradition called "hot packs," where about 1:72 packs contained only insert cards.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer's Ultra Gold Medallion parallel insert set also started in 1995, and were inserted one per pack.
Acquisitions and later days
In 1997, Ultra introduced the Platinum Medallion insert set, which was serial numbered to 100.
Acquisitions and later days
1998 saw the introduction of one-of-one purple Ultra Masterpieces, and started including short printed cards in the regular Gold and Platinum sets.
Acquisitions and later days
Comic book company Marvel Entertainment purchased the company on July 24, 1992, for US$540 million.
Acquisitions and later days
Marvel purchased another card company, SkyBox International, on March 8, 1995, for $150 million.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer began production of a super premium flagship set, called Flair, in 1993.
Acquisitions and later days
Flair was printed on very thick card stock, about twice the thickness of regular cards, and used a unique glossy finish and six color printing.
Acquisitions and later days
Marvel entered bankruptcy in 1996 along with its subsidiaries.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer was directly hurt by the 1994 Major League Baseball strike and prolonged lockouts in the NBA.
Acquisitions and later days
In June 1997, Marvel formed its Marvel Enterprise division, headed by president and CEO Scott C.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer was placed on the market by Marvel at an asking price of $30 million.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer exited bankruptcy, along with the rest of the Marvel group, on October 1, 1998.
Acquisitions and later days
In February 1999, Fleer/Skybox was sold to a corporation owned by Alex Grass and his son Roger.
Acquisitions and later days
Fleer acquired a license deal from WWE to produce and distribute WWE trading cards from 2001 to 2004.
Acquisitions and later days

In early 2005, Fleer announced that it would cease all productions of trading cards and file an Assignment for the Benefit of Creditors, which is a State Court liquidation, similar to Chapter 7 bankruptcy.
Acquisitions and later days
In July 2005, Upper Deck acquired the rights to the Fleer name and began producing Fleer-branded basketball, ice hockey and American football cards.
Acquisitions and later days
The $6.1 million Upper Deck paid for the Fleer name was significantly less than the $25 million they had offered to buy out Fleer a year earlier.
Acquisitions and later days
In 2006, Upper Deck produced baseball sets under the names Fleer, Fleer Ultra, Fleer Tradition, Flair, Skybox Autographics and Fleer Greats of the Game.
Acquisitions and later days
The last Fleer-branded baseball cards appeared in 2007.
Bill Ripken card
In 1989, Bill Ripken's Fleer card showed him holding a bat with the expletive "fuck face" written in plain view on the knob of the bat.
Bill Ripken card
Fleer subsequently rushed to correct the error, and in its haste, released versions in which the text was scrawled over with a marker, whited out with correction fluid, and also airbrushed.
Bill Ripken card
As of February 2009 the white out version has a book value of $120, but has been sold in mint condition on eBay for asking prices as high as $400.

The Patriots finished the season 12–4 to earn the second seed in the AFC and a first-round bye.
2014: Fourth Super Bowl win
Brady clinched his NFL record 12th AFC East division title with a Week 14 win against the San Diego Chargers, later in the season.
2014: Fourth Super Bowl win

In a 35–31 Divisional Round win over the Ravens, Brady threw for three touchdowns and ran in a fourth, breaking Curtis Martin's club record for rushing touchdowns in the playoffs; Brady also broke Joe Montana's record for playoff touchdowns with 46.
2014: Fourth Super Bowl win
After the Ravens scored on their first two possessions, the Patriots were quickly down 14–0, but would end up tying the game 14–14.
2014: Fourth Super Bowl win
Brady got the ball back, and threw a 23-yard touchdown to wide receiver Brandon LaFell to give the Patriots their first lead, 35–31, with 5:13 remaining.
2016: Fifth Super Bowl win
The following week, Brady and the Patriots defeated the Los Angeles Rams by a score of 26–10, giving Brady his record-201st career victory, including playoff games.
2016: Fifth Super Bowl win

Brady ended the regular season with 28 passing touchdowns and only two interceptions for the regular season, breaking the previous TD:INT ratio record of Nick Foles's 27:2 figure set in 2013 with the Eagles.
2016: Fifth Super Bowl win
Brady was also ranked first on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2017 as the best player in the league, becoming the first player to be named as #1 twice since the listing began.
2016: Fifth Super Bowl win
Brady completed 18-of-38 passes for 287 yards, two touchdowns, and two interceptions as the Patriots won 34–16, clinching a record sixth consecutive trip to the AFC Championship Game.
2016: Fifth Super Bowl win

With the victory, Brady won his fifth Super Bowl, which set a record for most Super Bowl victories of any quarterback in history and tied defensive player Charles Haley for the most Super Bowl victories for any player.
2017: Third MVP and loss in Super Bowl LII

In Week 2, Brady's three touchdown passes and 447 passing yards in a 36–20 win over the New Orleans Saints earned him his 28th AFC Offensive Player of the Week award, breaking the record previously held by Peyton Manning for the most AFC Offensive Player of the Week awards in a career.
2017: Third MVP and loss in Super Bowl LII
Brady obtained his 187th career win, setting the record for most regular season wins in NFL history.
2017: Third MVP and loss in Super Bowl LII
Brady completed 28-of-48 attempts for three passing touchdowns, no interceptions, and a Super Bowl record 505 yards–which set a new postseason game record for the most passing yards in NFL history.
2017: Third MVP and loss in Super Bowl LII
The Eagles recovered the fumble and cemented their 41–33 win with a field goal, securing their first franchise Super Bowl victory in a game with the most combined total yardage in NFL history.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England

In Week 5, in a 38–24 win against the Colts, Brady's 500th career touchdown pass went to Josh Gordon, who became the 71st different player to catch a touchdown from Brady, breaking a record previously held by Vinny Testaverde.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
In Week 6, in a 43–40 win against the Chiefs, Brady secured his 200th career regular season win, making him the only quarterback in NFL history to accomplish that feat.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
During Week 16 against the Bills, Brady was limited to 126 passing yards, but the Patriots won 24–12, clinching the AFC East pennant for the 10th consecutive season and 16th time in 18 years.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
In Week 17, Brady helped the Patriots clinch a first-round bye, with a 38–3 win against the Jets.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
In Super Bowl LIII, Brady completed 21-of-35 passes for 262 passing yards and an interception as the Patriots won 13–3 over the Rams in the lowest-scoring Super Bowl in history.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
On August 4, 2019, Brady signed a two-year contract extension worth $70 million through the 2021 season; the terms of the contract allowed Brady to become a free agent after the 2019 season.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England
Against the 2019 Patriots salary cap, Brady was the highest-paid player on the team at $21.5 million.
2018–2019: Sixth Super Bowl win and final season in New England

Although the Patriots finished the regular season with a 12–4 record and won the AFC East for the 11th consecutive year, this loss, combined with a win by the Chiefs, denied New England a first-round bye for the first time since 2009.
2020 season: Seventh Super Bowl win
The two-year contract was worth $50 million in fully guaranteed money, with up to $4.5 million each year in incentives.
2020 season: Seventh Super Bowl win

Brady's five touchdowns in the Buccaneers' 38–31 win against the Chargers marked the seventh time in his career he had five touchdowns in a game and, at age 43, made him the oldest quarterback to have a five-touchdown game.
2020 season: Seventh Super Bowl win

In Week 16 against the Lions, Brady completed 22-of-27 attempts with 348 yards, four touchdowns, and a perfect passer rating of 158.3 in the first half before being rested in the second half of the 47–7 victory.
2020 season: Seventh Super Bowl win
Brady extended his record for most Super Bowl wins by a player with his seventh and extended his record for Super Bowl MVP awards, with five.
2021 season
On February 11, 2021, it was revealed that Brady had knee discomfort through most of the 2020 season and would require a minor arthroscopy for a routine cleanup.
2021 season
In Week 3, against the Rams, Brady threw for 432 yards, and had two touchdowns, and joined Drew Brees as the only players in NFL history to record 80,000 passing yards during the 34–24 loss.
2021 season
In Week 7, Brady became the first quarterback in NFL history to record 600 touchdown passes, with a nine-yard pass to Evans in a win against the Chicago Bears.
2021 season
Brady became the oldest player in NFL history to pass for at least 5,000 yards and his passing yards total marked the third-most for a single season in NFL history.
Initial retirement
In Brady's first two years with Tampa, the Buccaneers posted a regular season record of 24–9, which were the two most successful back-to-back seasons in franchise history.
Initial retirement
Their 13–4 regular season record in 2021 was the best result in franchise history, eclipsing the 12–4 record of the 2002 Super Bowl winning team.
Initial retirement
Prior to Brady's arrival, the franchise had an all-time playoff record of 6–9; at the time of Brady's retirement, the all-time playoff record for Tampa Bay stood at 11–10.

In Week 18 against the Falcons, Brady broke his own NFL record for completions in a season, as well as Matthew Stafford's 2012 record for pass attempts in a season.
Broadcasting career
Brady's deal with Fox will reportedly pay him $375 million over 10 years, making Brady the highest paid sports commentator in history.

Brady earned around $44 million from endorsements as of 2025.

In 2023, it was reported Brady owned 1 million shares in FTX, and he and his wife lost an estimated combined value of $45 million when FTX went bankrupt.

name: Joe Namath

caption: Namath as a rookie with the New York Jets in 1965

New York Jets Ring of Honor

sents: lead

Joseph William Namath (;; born May 31, 1943) is an American former professional football quarterback who played in the American Football League (AFL) and National Football League (NFL) for 13 seasons, primarily with the New York Jets.
lead
Nicknamed "Broadway Joe", he played college football for the Alabama Crimson Tide, receiving first-team All-SEC honors and winning the national championship in 1964.
lead
Namath was selected by the Jets first overall in the 1965 AFL draft.
lead
During his five AFL seasons, Namath was a two-time MVP and twice led the league in passing yards, while winning one AFL championship and one Super Bowl.
lead
Both victories remain the Jets' only championships.
lead
Following the 1970 AFL–NFL merger, Namath joined the NFL with the Jets, earning Pro Bowl and second-team All-Pro honors in 1972 after leading the league in passing yards and passing touchdowns.
lead
He played in New York for seven more seasons and spent his final year as a member of the Los Angeles Rams.
lead
Namath cemented his legacy in 1969 when he guaranteed his heavy underdog Jets would win Super Bowl III before defeating the NFL's Baltimore Colts in one of the greatest sports upsets of all time.
Early life
Namath was born and raised in Beaver Falls, Pennsylvania, 30 miles (50 km) northwest of Pittsburgh.
Early life
He later clarified a story about being the only white player on his high school basketball team on The James Brown Show in 2018, where he was the guest.
Early life
Namath stated that although he was one of several white players on the team, he was the only white starter.
Early life
Coached by Larry Bruno at Beaver Falls, Namath's football team won the WPIAL Class AA championship with a 9–0 record in 1960.
Early life
Upon graduating from high school in 1961, Namath received offers from several Major League Baseball teams, including the Yankees, Indians, Reds, Pirates, and Phillies, but football prevailed.
Early life
However, a college degree was finally conferred on Namath at age 64, after he completed an external-program Bachelor of Arts degree in interdisciplinary studies at the University of Alabama in 2007.
College career
Between 1962 and 1964, Namath quarterbacked the Alabama Crimson Tide program under Bryant and his offensive coordinator, Howard Schnellenberger.
College career
A year after being suspended for the final two games of the regular season, Namath led the Tide to a national championship in 1964.
College career
During his time at the University of Alabama, Namath led the team to a 29–4 record over three seasons.
College career
When Namath was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1985, he teared up during his induction speech upon mentioning Bryant, who had died of a heart attack two years prior.
College career
Namath attended college at the height of the civil rights movement (1955–1968) in the South, and was present when Governor George Wallace stood at the school's auditorium.
College career
In 1964, despite suffering a nagging knee injury in the fourth game of his senior year at Alabama, Namath limped through the undefeated regular season to the Orange Bowl.
College career
The cartilage damage to Namath's right knee later designated him class 4-F for the military draft, a deferment from service during the Vietnam War.
College career
Namath was eleventh in the voting for the 1964 Heisman Trophy, which was won by quarterback John Huarte of Notre Dame.
Professional career
In late 1964, the then still separate NFL and upstart AFL were at the height of their bidding war, and held their respective drafts on the same day, November 28.
Professional career
Namath was a first-round draft selection by both leagues: the St.
Professional career
Louis Cardinals selected him 12th overall in the 1965 NFL draft, while the Jets made him the first overall pick in the AFL draft.
Professional career
When meeting with executives of the Cardinals, Namath's salary request was $200,000 and a new Lincoln Continental.
Professional career

While initially surprised at his demands, the Cardinals told Namath they would agree to his terms only if he would sign before the Orange Bowl, which would have made Namath ineligible to play in the game.
Professional career
The day after the Orange Bowl, he elected to sign with the Jets, under the direction of Sonny Werblin, for a salary of US$427,000 over three years (a pro football record at the time).
Professional career
Offensive tackle Sherman Plunkett came up with the nickname "Broadway Joe" in 1965, following Namath's appearance on the cover of Sports Illustrated in July.
Professional career
Namath would eventually be on the cover of Sports Illustrated 22 times.
New York Jets
In Namath's rookie season the 1965 Jets were winless in their first six games with him splitting time with second-year quarterback Mike Taliaferro.
New York Jets
With Namath starting full-time they won five of the last eight of a fourteen-game season and Namath was named the AFL Rookie of the year.
New York Jets

Namath became the first professional quarterback to pass for 4,000 yards in a season when he threw for 4,007 yards during a 14-game season in 1967, a record broken by Dan Fouts in a 16-game season in 1979 (4,082).
New York Jets
Nicholas, Namath was an AFL All-Star in 1965, 1967, 1968, and 1969.
New York Jets
In the 1968 AFL title game, Namath threw three touchdowns to lead New York to a 27–23 victory over the defending AFL champion Oakland Raiders.
New York Jets
Namath was an AFC–NFC Pro Bowler in 1972, is a member of the Jets' and the American Football League's All-Time Team, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1985.
New York Jets

In 1967, Namath led the AFL in yards per passing attempt (8.2), and repeated this again in the NFL in 1972 (8.7), making him the only player in history to lead both leagues in yards per passing attempt in a season.
Super Bowl III
The high point of Namath's career was his performance in the Jets' 16–7 victory over the Baltimore Colts in Super Bowl III in January 1969, shortly before the AFL–NFL merger.
Super Bowl III

The first two interleague championship games had resulted in blowout victories for the NFL's Green Bay Packers, and sports writers from NFL cities insisted the AFL would take several more years to be truly competitive.
Super Bowl III
Namath was the Super Bowl MVP, completing eight passes to George Sauer Jr. alone for 133 yards.
Super Bowl III
The win made him the first quarterback to start and win a national championship game in college, a major professional league championship, and a Super Bowl.
Super Bowl III

When he was asked by reporters after the game whether the Colts' defense was the "toughest he had ever faced", Namath responded, "That would be the Buffalo Bills' defense." The AFL-worst Bills had intercepted Namath five times, three for touchdowns, in their only win in 1968 in late September.
Later career with the Jets
After not missing a single game because of injury in his first five years in the league, Namath played in just 28 of 58 possible games between 1970 and 1973 because of various injuries.
Later career with the Jets
After winning division championships in 1968 and 1969, the Jets struggled to records of 4–10, 6–8, 7–7, and 4–10.
Later career with the Jets
His most memorable moment in those four seasons came on September 24, 1972, when he and his boyhood idol Johnny Unitas combined for 872 passing yards in Baltimore.
Later career with the Jets

Namath threw for 496 yards and six touchdowns on only 15 completions and Unitas 376 yards and three touchdowns in a 44–34 New York victory over the Colts, its first against Baltimore since Super Bowl III.
Later career with the Jets
Another notable moment was in 1970, when the head of ABC's televised sports, Roone Arledge, made sure that Monday Night Football inaugural game on September 21, featured Namath.
Later career with the Jets
The Jets met the Cleveland Browns in Cleveland Municipal Stadium in front of both a record crowd of 85,703 and a huge television audience.
Later career with the Jets
The Chicago Winds of the World Football League (WFL) made an overture to Namath prior to the start of its 1975 season.
Later career with the Jets
First, they designed their uniforms nearly identically to that of the Jets, dropping red and going with green and white, to allow Namath to continue marketing his number 12 jersey in Jets colors.
Later career with the Jets

Then they offered Namath a contract worth $600,000 a year for three years; a $2 million annuity ($100,000 per year for 20 years); a $500,000 signing bonus; and terms for Namath's eventual ownership of a WFL franchise.
Later career with the Jets
Upon this development, Namath, in turn, requested the lofty sum of 15 percent of the entire league's television revenue, which was rejected by the league.
Los Angeles Rams
After 12 years with the Jets, Namath was waived prior to the 1977 season to facilitate a move to the Los Angeles Rams when a trade could not be worked out.
Los Angeles Rams
Signing on May 12, Namath hoped to revitalize his career, but knee injuries, a bad hamstring, and the general ravages of 13 years as a quarterback in professional football had taken their toll.
Los Angeles Rams

After playing well in a 2–1 start, Namath took a beating in a one-point road-loss on a cold, windy, and rainy Monday Night Football game against the Chicago Bears, throwing four interceptions and having a fifth nullified by a penalty.
Acting career
Building on his brief success as a host on 1969's The Joe Namath Show, Namath transitioned into an acting career.
Acting career

He starred in several movies, including C.C. and Company with Ann-Margret and William Smith in 1970, appeared on stage in "Picnic" with Donna Mills in 1971 and was in a brief 1978 television series, The Waverly Wonders.
Acting career
Namath was a candidate to host the 1988 revival of the American game show Family Feud, before the job went to comedian Ray Combs.
Acting career
In September 2012, Namath was honored by the Ride of Fame and a double-decker tour bus was dedicated to him in New York City.
Acting career
He appeared as himself in the 2013 sports film Underdogs and the 2015 comedy film The Wedding Ringer.
Personal life

Namath was the only athlete listed on the master list of Richard Nixon's political opponents, which was made public in 1973 during the Watergate investigation, erroneously listed as playing for the New York Giants.
Personal life
White House Counsel John Dean claimed not to know why Namath was included on the list and suggested that it might have been a mistake.
Personal life
Namath addressed this on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson on July 20, 1973.
Personal life
While taking a voice class in 1983, Namath met Deborah Mays, who later changed her first name to May and then changed it again to Tatiana, an aspiring actress; he was 39 and she was 22.
Personal life

They married in 1984, with Namath claiming, "She caught my last pass." The longtime bachelor became a dedicated family man when the couple had two children, Jessica (born 1986) and Olivia (born 1991).
Personal life
The couple divorced in 2000, with the children living in Florida with their father.
Personal life
By 1987, Namath was able to stop his drinking, though he would relapse after his divorce in 2000.
Personal life
On December 20, 2003, Namath garnered unfavorable publicity after he consumed too much alcohol during a day that was dedicated to the Jets' announcement of their All-Time team.
Personal life
In 2019, Namath said he used the incident as motivation to quit alcohol, explaining "I had embarrassed my friends and family and could not escape that feeling.
Personal life
In July 2015, Namath joined the search for two boys who disappeared during a fishing trip off the coast of Florida, and offered a $100,000 reward for the safe return of the boys.
Personal life
On June 6, 2018, Namath threw out the first pitch at a Chicago Cubs baseball game at Wrigley Field.
Bachelors III

After the Super Bowl victory in 1969, Namath opened a popular Upper East Side nightclub called Bachelors III, which not only drew big names in sports, entertainment, and politics, but also organized crime.
Bachelors III
Namath refused, apparently retiring from football during a teary news conference, but he eventually recanted and agreed to sell the club, and reported to the Jets in time for the 1969–70 season.
Bachelors III
Namath again threatened to retire before the 1970 and 1971 seasons; New York wrote in 1971 that "his retirement act had become shallow and predictable".
Media and advertising icon

Namath's prowess on the field, fashion sense, lighthearted personality, and status as a sex symbol made him the first sports figure to appeal equally to men, women, and children—as demonstrated by his various product endorsements over the years.
Media and advertising icon

The white shoes started when Namath was at Alabama, where he kept having his worn-out cleats taped over as a superstition, especially after his first major knee injury was the result of a game in which he had forgotten to have the shoes taped.
Media and advertising icon

Namath also appeared in television advertisements both during and after his playing career, most notably for Ovaltine milk flavoring, Noxzema shaving cream (in which he was shaved by a then-unknown Farrah Fawcett), and Hanes Beautymist pantyhose (which he famously wore in the commercials).
Media and advertising icon
In 2011, Namath was representing Topps and promoting a "Super Bowl Legends" contest, appearing on its behalf on the Late Show with David Letterman.
Media and advertising icon
On June 2, 2013, Namath was the guest speaker at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, unveiling the Canton, Ohio museum's $27 million expansion and renovation plan.
Media and advertising icon
As of 2018, Namath is the spokesperson for the insurance agency Medicare Coverage Helpline.
Biographies
In November 2006, the book Namath: A Biography by Mark Kriegel was published, reaching the New York Times extended bestseller list.
Biographies
In conjunction with its release, Namath was interviewed for the November 19, 2006, edition of CBS' 60 Minutes.
Biographies
In 2009, 40 years after winning Super Bowl III, he presented the Vince Lombardi Trophy to the Pittsburgh Steelers, who won Super Bowl XLIII.
